title: Inherited Roth IRA Rules and Deadlines (October 2026)
summary: This guide covers inherited Roth IRA rules as of October 2026, including tax treatment, deadlines, and withdrawal choices for beneficiaries.
body_markdown:
When a Roth IRA owner dies, the beneficiaries who inherit the account follow set withdrawal rules. Which rules apply depends on the beneficiary's relationship to the owner and the year the owner died. This guide covers key points for beneficiaries and families to be aware of, including: what an inherited Roth IRA is, the SECURE Act and SECURE 2.0, beneficiary categories, exceptions to the 10-Year Rule, tax matters, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Most non-spouse heirs must empty an inherited Roth IRA by December 31 of year 10 after death.
- Inherited Roth IRAs under the 10-year rule require no annual withdrawals before the deadline.
- Inherited Roth earnings may be taxable before the owner's five-year holding period ends.
- Elayne tracks inherited IRA deadlines, helps locate accounts, and shares records with advisors.


## What Is an Inherited Roth IRA?


An inherited Roth IRA is a Roth retirement account received after its owner dies. Beneficiary withdrawal rules differ from those for a Roth IRA funded by its owner.


Non-spouse beneficiaries must follow[inherited IRA distribution rules](https://www.elayne.com/resources/inherited-ira-distribution-rules) and keep the account separate from their own IRAs and cannot contribute to it. A surviving spouse may qualify to treat the inherited Roth IRA as their own.

## How the SECURE Act and SECURE 2.0 Changed Inherited Roth IRA Rules


For deaths before 2020, many beneficiaries could spread withdrawals over their life expectancy. For later deaths,[IRS beneficiary rules](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-beneficiary) apply the SECURE Act’s 10-year deadline to most non-spouse beneficiaries.


SECURE 2.0 reduced penalties for missed required withdrawals, including those from inherited Roth IRAs:


- The penalty is 25% of the shortfall.
- A reduced 10% penalty applies when the missed amount is withdrawn and applicable tax-return requirements are met within the IRS correction window.


## Beneficiary Categories


Category Who qualifies Withdrawal schedule


Eligible designated beneficiary Spouse; owner’s minor child; disabled or chronically ill person; someone no more than 10 years younger Conditional life-expectancy options


Designated beneficiary Other named individuals Generally 10 years


Non-designated beneficiary Estates, charities, trusts failing look-through requirements Generally five years


## Inherited Roth IRA Rules for Surviving Spouses


A surviving spouse who is the sole beneficiary can treat the Roth IRA as their own, roll it into an existing Roth IRA, or keep it inherited.


Under[IRS inherited Roth IRA rules](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590b) , inherited status preserves penalty-free access before age 59½ and may delay beneficiary RMDs if the deceased was younger. Tax-free withdrawals still depend on the five-year rule. Inherited status can allow access without an early-withdrawal penalty, even when some earnings remain taxable.


## Inherited Roth IRA Rules for Non-Spouse Beneficiaries


Non-spouse beneficiaries without eligible designated beneficiary status generally must empty an inherited Roth IRA by December 31 of year 10, counting from the year after death.


Unlike inherited traditional IRAs whose owners died on or after their required beginning date, this group’s inherited Roth IRAs require no annual RMDs during that window. Beneficiaries can choose withdrawal timing within the deadline.


## Exceptions to the 10-Year Rule for Inherited Roth IRAs


Eligible designated beneficiaries can generally take life-expectancy withdrawals:


- Surviving spouses.
- The owner’s child under age 21.
- Individuals meeting IRS disability or chronic illness criteria.
- People no more than 10 years younger than the owner, including older beneficiaries.


Under the[IRS rules for an owner's minor child](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590b) , the life-expectancy option eventually gives way to a final payout deadline:


- The 10-year countdown starts when the child turns 21.
- Full withdrawal is due by the end of the year the child turns 31.


## Are Inherited Roth IRAs Taxable?


Qualified inherited Roth IRA distributions are generally free of federal income tax. If the owner’s five-year holding period has not been met, earnings withdrawn may be taxable. State income tax treatment varies.


## Inherited Roth IRA vs. Inherited Traditional IRA: Key Differences


Feature Inherited Roth IRA Inherited traditional IRA


Federal withdrawal taxes Qualified withdrawals are tax-free Ordinary income, except after-tax basis


Original owner's lifetime required minimum distributions (RMDs) None Required when applicable


Accelerated payouts Qualified withdrawals add no taxable income Taxable withdrawals can raise tax brackets


Qualified inherited Roth IRA withdrawals are free of federal income tax, while inherited traditional IRA withdrawals generally count as ordinary income except for amounts attributable to after-tax contributions. Roth earnings may still be taxable if the original owner's five-year holding period has not been met.


## Penalties for Missing RMDs on an Inherited Roth IRA


- Missed required withdrawals carry a 25% penalty on the shortfall.
- Correcting the shortfall within the IRS correction window, generally two years, can reduce the penalty to 10%.


After correction, beneficiaries can request a reasonable-cause waiver using Form 5329 with an explanation.

## How Elayne Helps Beneficiaries Manage Inherited Roth IRA Deadlines


[Elayne](https://www.elayne.com/company) is an online operating layer for settling an estate after a death. For inherited Roth IRAs, Elayne tracks the final withdrawal deadline, helps locate retirement accounts, and keeps related records in one shared estate overview.


### How Elayne Tracks the Final Deadline


An inherited Roth IRA under the 10-year rule has a fixed final date: December 31 of the tenth year after the owner's death. Elayne records that date in the estate overview, so it stays visible next to other estate dates. A worked example shows how the date is counted:


- Owner's date of death: March 2026.
- First year of the 10-year count: 2027, the year after death.
- Final deadline to empty the account: December 31, 2036.


In practice, the deadline depends on the calendar year of death, not the exact date of death.


Surviving spouses and other eligible designated beneficiaries may follow a different schedule. A tax professional can confirm which category applies, and Elayne tracks the dates tied to that schedule once the category is known.


### How Elayne Helps Locate Retirement Accounts


Elayne's Verified Asset Search looks across financial sources, including state unclaimed-property registries, for accounts that may belong to the estate. Document analysis reviews tax returns, bank statements, and other records for clues about retirement distributions and the institutions that hold accounts.


### How Elayne Shares Records With Advisors


Authorized family members,[co-executors](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-does-an-executor-of-a-will-actually-do-a-complete-guide-to-executor-duties) , financial advisors, tax professionals, and[attorneys](https://www.elayne.com/resources/teaming-up-how-elayne-and-attorneys-help-families-after-a-loss) can work from one shared dashboard with role-based permissions. Documents sit in one estate record instead of separate email threads. Records that custodians and tax professionals commonly request include:


- The death certificate.
- The beneficiary designation or claim form.
- Account statements showing the date-of-death value.
- Roth IRA contribution records

## FAQ


### How is the original owner’s five-year holding period documented under IRS inherited Roth IRA rules?


The original owner’s Roth IRA contribution records, account statements, and Forms 5498 can help confirm when the holding period began. The beneficiary's custodian or tax professional can review those records, including records from earlier custodians if the account moved. The inheritance date alone does not prove whether earnings qualify for tax-free withdrawal.


### How do the rules work when an inherited Roth IRA is split among siblings or other beneficiaries?


An account with several named beneficiaries can be divided into separate inherited accounts, generally by December 31 of the year after the owner's death. Each beneficiary then follows the rules for their own category and chooses their own withdrawal timing.


Without separate accounts, life-expectancy payouts are generally based on the oldest beneficiary. Beneficiaries under the 10-year rule share the same final deadline: December 31 of the tenth year after the owner's death.


### Can a beneficiary name a successor beneficiary on an inherited Roth IRA?


Yes. Custodians generally allow a beneficiary to name a successor on an inherited account. If no successor is named, the custodian's default provisions generally apply.


A successor beneficiary generally cannot extend the original schedule. When the first beneficiary was under the 10-year rule, the account must still be empty by December 31 of the tenth year after the original owner's death. When the first beneficiary was taking life-expectancy withdrawals, the successor generally must empty the account within 10 years after that beneficiary's death.


### Do states tax inherited Roth IRA withdrawals?


State treatment varies. Many states with an income tax follow the federal treatment of qualified Roth IRA distributions, and some states do not levy an income tax at all.


A small number of states also have an inheritance or estate tax, which can apply to account value separately from income tax. A state tax agency or tax professional can confirm the rule for a specific state.


### How are inherited Roth IRA withdrawals reported on a tax return?


The custodian reports distributions on Form 1099-R, which is issued in the beneficiary's name. Qualified distributions are generally reported with a taxable amount of zero on Form 1040.


Form 8606 is used to calculate the taxable part of a distribution that is not qualified. Form 5329 is used for a missed required withdrawal.
